recent_posts.title: Measuring Model Quantisation Quality with KL Divergence
recent_posts.summary: KL divergence (KLD) is used to measure how much a quantised LLM deviates from a bf16 reference, providing a better quality signal than perplexity by isolating quantisation damage. Using the mlx-kld tool, six MLX quantisations of Qwen 3.6 27B (dense) and five of Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B (MoE) are benchmarked across 65,536 tokens from WikiText-2. Key findings: 8-bit is effectively a bf16 drop-in; 6-bit RTN and oQ6 are statistically tied for the dense model; Unsloth Dynamic 4-bit is a poor deal at 8.6 effective bpw with worse quality than 6-bit; for the MoE model, DWQ-4bit beats oQ4 by ~34% because it protects router tensors; quant rankings don't generalise between dense and MoE architectures. The mlx-kld tool caches reference log-probs as a sparse top-K structure (~420x compression) and loads only one model at a time, making multi-quant comparisons practical on Apple Silicon.

recent_posts.title: Agentic Coding Tools
recent_posts.summary: A structured comparison of seven agentic coding tools — Claude Code, Cline, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, Google Antigravity, Cursor, and Amazon Kiro — evaluated across functionality, developer experience, configuration management, automation, access control, and estimated monthly cost. Claude Code and Cline lead in coding ability, speed, and RBAC features, while tools like Amazon Kiro and Google Antigravity lag in autonomy and require more babysitting. Monthly costs range from ~$100 for Claude Code to $1,200–$2,200 for Cline depending on usage.

recent_posts.title: LLM FAQ
recent_posts.summary: A practical FAQ covering common questions about running LLMs locally. Key topics include: choosing between larger lower-quantized models vs smaller higher-quantized ones (larger wins), why F16 quantization is wasteful for text generation, how to think about LLM-generated code quality (treat it like human code with review processes), whether AI will take jobs (nuanced maybe), and a detailed explanation of why Ollama is not just a llama.cpp wrapper — covering its model hot-loading, parallelization, memory management, OpenAI-compatible API, and multi-modal support features.

recent_posts.title: Getting started with Claude Code configuration and workflow tips
recent_posts.summary: Practical setup and workflow advice for getting started with Claude Code, covering configuration (CLAUDE.md rules, sandboxing, permissions, hooks), extending capabilities (skills, LSP integration, MCP tools), and workflow patterns (planning mode, fresh sessions, reusable commands). Emphasizes keeping context lean, using layered rules, pre-approving safe operations while hard-blocking dangerous ones, and planning before acting.

recent_posts.title: Patching NVIDIA's driver and vLLM to enable P2P on consumer GPUs
recent_posts.summary: NVIDIA artificially restricts peer-to-peer (P2P) GPU communication on consumer cards like the RTX 3090 via a software limitation. By patching the open-source NVIDIA kernel driver (aikitoria/open-gpu-kernel-modules) and bypassing vLLM's hardcoded P2P capability check, it's possible to enable direct GPU-to-GPU DMA transfers on consumer hardware. Combined with a tuned fused MoE Triton kernel config for the RTX 3090, running Qwen 3.5 35b on dual RTX 3090s yields 10-30% throughput improvement over the unpatched setup. The post covers IOMMU passthrough configuration, driver installation, vLLM Dockerfile patching, fused_moe kernel tuning, expert parallelism benchmarks, and full Docker Compose and llama.cpp configurations.

recent_posts.title: The Role Bridging Problem
recent_posts.summary: AI tools enable people to produce work outside their domain expertise, but functional correctness doesn't equal domain quality. Code runs, tests pass, interfaces render — yet architectural considerations, edge case handling, and maintainability concerns are missing. This leads to technical debt accumulation, knowledge fragmentation, review fatigue, and false velocity. The solution isn't restricting AI use but applying critical thinking to outputs, involving domain experts when working outside your expertise, using MCP tools to ground AI in domain-specific knowledge, and recognizing when you can't properly evaluate what AI generates.

recent_posts.title: Stop Polluting Context - Let Users Disable Individual MCP Tools
recent_posts.summary: MCP servers expose many tools that consume significant context window tokens — often 32k+ tokens just for tool descriptions before any code is written. The post argues MCP server developers should implement selective tool disabling via environment variables, allowing users to exclude tools they don't need. This reduces token usage, improves model reliability (less context rot), shrinks attack surface, and enables compliance controls. Two implementation patterns are shown: simple conditional registration (Python) and registry-based runtime filtering (Go). GitHub's MCP server is called out as the worst offender, consuming 46k tokens across 91 tools with no disable mechanism.

recent_posts.title: MCP DevTools
recent_posts.summary: MCP DevTools is a single Go binary that consolidates 10-15 separate MCP servers into one modular server for AI coding agents. Built with a tool registry pattern, it supports STDIO and HTTP transport modes and provides tools for web search, GitHub access, package version checking, library documentation, filesystem operations, document processing, SBOM generation, vulnerability scanning, and more. A configurable security middleware layer inspects externally fetched content before it reaches the LLM, helping mitigate prompt injection attacks. Optional tools include Claude, Gemini, and AWS Q Developer agent integrations for multi-agent workflows. Installation is a single `go install` command.

recent_posts.title: Vibe Coding vs Agentic Coding
recent_posts.summary: A comparison of vibe coding and agentic coding approaches to AI-assisted development. Vibe coding is framed as creative, experimental, and accessible but unsuitable for production systems. Agentic coding is presented as a disciplined engineering practice where AI agents work as development peers with proper tooling, context, and constraints via MCP servers. The post outlines a Setup→Plan→Act→Review workflow, provides a detailed contrast table across dimensions like maintainability, security, and scalability, and offers practical advice for transitioning from vibe to agentic coding in professional settings.

recent_posts.title: My Plan, Document, Act, Review flow for Agentic Software Development
recent_posts.summary: A practical workflow for AI-assisted software development using a Setup → Plan → Act → Review & Iterate cycle. The author describes how to configure AI coding agents (specifically Cline) with rules and MCP tools, create structured development plan documents, manage context across sessions, and iteratively refine both code and agent rules. Includes concrete prompt templates for creating development plans and guiding agents through phased implementation.
